title: Your sunset

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heavy hour: Antony's angel plaiting rope, then praying, then plaiting again. The afternoon is held. Now the light starts to go.
screen: `THE HEAVY HOUR.` → `THE LIGHT STARTS TO GO.`

segments.voice: Phones go up on every balcony when the sky turns orange. Early Christians did something with that hour too. Basil of Caesarea, a bishop, wrote that the fathers thought it right not to receive the gift of the evening light in silence, but to give thanks the moment it appeared. And he mentions an old hymn the people sang at the lighting of the lamps, a hymn so old he couldn't say who had written it.
screen: `EVERYONE FILMS THE SUNSET.` → `NOT IN SILENCE.` → `A HYMN AT THE LIGHTING OF THE LAMPS.`

segments.voice: Today's question: why mark the sunset at all? The Christian answer lives in that lamp-lighting hymn, known by its Greek name, Phos Hilaron, joyful light. It greets Christ as the joyful light of the Father's glory, and, coming to the setting of the sun and seeing the evening light, praises Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It is still sung at Vespers, the evening prayer, in Orthodox churches. That's the teaching: in Christian evening prayer, sunset isn't only the day ending. The lamp you light becomes thanks for a light that stays. Now a neighbor, in its own terms. In Islam the day's prayers follow the sun's path, and one of them, maghrib, is prayed just after sunset. The Qur'an asks for prayer at the two ends of the day and in some watches of the night. What's shared: neither tradition lets the light go without turning to God, right at the hinge of the day. An honest difference: the Phos Hilaron is a hymn sung to Christ as the light itself, within the Christian faith in the Trinity; maghrib is a set prayer to God, facing Mecca, with bowing and prostration, prayed in the same form every evening. Two ways of meeting dusk, each in its own house, neither standing in for the other. On your own path, sunset can become a small rite of yours, with its sources named: one light switched on, one breath of thanks, the day turning.
screen: `WHY MARK THE SUNSET?` · `PHOS HILARON: JOYFUL LIGHT.` · `MAGHRIB, JUST AFTER SUNSET.` · `SHARED HINGE, DIFFERENT PRAYERS.` · then, large: `THE DAY TURNS.`

segments.voice: Look at one source of light near you: a window going gold, a lamp, a candle. Watch it for a few breaths and give it a quiet thank you, the way the old hymn greeted the lamp. Then close your eyes and keep the glow in mind.
Your sunset: a small rite at the hinge of the day. In the Phos Hilaron, thanks as the lamps are lit; in Islam, maghrib just after the sun goes down.
Here's the line for dusk: the day turns, and you turn toward the light. Good evening.
